content: The analysis of renal safety associated with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) in HIV-infected patients has been extensively studied. Research published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2010 (volume 51, pages 496–505) highlights the potential nephrotoxic effects of TDF. Fernandez-Fernandez et al. (2011) provided an updated review on tenofovir nephrotoxicity, emphasizing its clinical implications in AIDS Research and Treatment. Young et al. (2012) investigated renal function in HIV patients initiating TDF-based therapy combined with efavirenz, lopinavir, or atazanavir, as published in AIDS (volume 26, pages 567–575). Their findings underscored the importance of monitoring renal parameters in these patients. Mallett et al. (2015) conducted a systematic review on the accuracy of urine glucose dipstick testing for detecting renal toxicity in HIV patients on TDF, which was included in the WHO guidelines for chronic kidney disease evaluation and management. De Leon et al. (2015) demonstrated a strong correlation between protein reagent strip results and the protein-to-creatinine ratio for detecting renal dysfunction in HIV patients, as published in AIDS Research and Therapy. The World Health Organization (WHO) also conducted a systematic review in 2015 to assess the utility of glycosuria and proteinuria dipsticks for screening and monitoring tenofovir-associated tubulopathy in resource-limited settings. Van Lunzen et al. (2012) reported on the efficacy of once-daily dolutegravir in combination therapy for antiretroviral-naïve adults with HIV, with interim 48-week results from the SPRING-1 trial published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. Similarly, Raffi et al. (2013) compared dolutegravir to raltegravir in antiretroviral-naïve adults, with findings from the SPRING-2 study published in The Lancet (volume 381, pages 735–743). Eron et al. (2013) evaluated the safety and efficacy of dolutegravir in treatment-experienced patients with raltegravir-resistant HIV-1 infection, presenting 24-week results from the VIKING study in The Journal of Infectious Diseases. Koteff et al. (2012) conducted a phase 1 study to assess dolutegravir’s impact on renal function using iohexol and para-aminohippurate clearance in healthy subjects, published in British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. Cottrell et al. (2013) reviewed the pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and drug interaction profile of dolutegravir in Clinical Pharmacokinetics. Eron et al. (2013) also reported on the long-term efficacy and safety of raltegravir in the BENCHMRK studies, which evaluated its use over five years in treatment-experienced patients with drug-resistant HIV, as published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. Grinsztejn et al. (2014) explored the use of raltegravir in HIV and tuberculosis co-infected patients in the ANRS 12180 Reflate TB study, a phase 2 trial published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. The D:A:D study, as reported by Sabin et al. (2008) in The Lancet, examined the association between nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and myocardial infarction risk in HIV-infected patients. These studies collectively highlight the importance of monitoring renal function and other safety parameters in HIV patients receiving antiretroviral therapy, particularly those on tenofovir or integrase inhibitors like dolutegravir and raltegravir. They also underscore the need for personalized treatment strategies to optimize efficacy while minimizing adverse effects.
